doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The McKinney's book and its style
summary: Carter says the band already had a large book and he doesn't know how much he added; Berger finds the recordings nostalgic.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Do you recall the type of music that . . . you were musical director. Did that give you free reign as to what the band would play, or were you under any constraints as far as what McKinney wanted himself or what the bookers felt they needed or . . .

Well, I guess all of that played a part in what we did. In addition to that is the fact that they had quite a book, you know, when I joined them. How much I contributed to that book, I don’t know at this moment.
It always seemed to me there wasn’t much, I mean, in numbers.
No, I don’t think there was, too.
I’m just wondering why that was.
Well, they already had a sort of expansive book, you know.

The music, at least the recorded music of McKinney’s, I don’t know how to describe it. It’s very different from a band like Fletcher Henderson’s or Chick Webb’s at the time. It’s almost . . . sort of almost nostalgic; I don’t know; it’s the word that comes to mind . . . even for that time, you know, of something earlier. Maybe it’s just more quote, “commercial,” unquote. I don’t know.
Did you get any feeling of that, that this was a different kind of . . . they were looking for a different kind of market or something with this band?
Then again, the recordings may not be indicative of what was played in the . . .
Certainly not of everything that was played, no.
